Look at these two observations:
A sharp nail pierces a wooden board easily, but a blunt nail does not.
A camel walks on sand without sinking, but a thin-legged goat sinks into the same sand.
THINK ON YOUR OWN  What is the same about these two situations? What is different? Write one idea in your notebook.
Turn to your partner. Share your idea and listen to theirs. Together, agree on one explanation for why the sharp nail and the camel do not sink or struggle.
Be ready to share your pair's explanation with the class.

CHAPTER  Force and Pressure
TOPIC  Effects of Force, Pressure and Applications in Everyday Life
SDG GOAL  Goal 9 — Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure

✓
Explain how force can change the speed, direction, or shape of an object, using everyday examples.
✓
Describe pressure as force acting per unit area and demonstrate how surface area affects pressure through simple experiments.
✓
Differentiate between contact and non-contact forces and identify practical examples of each.

✓
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
✓
MUST  Explain, with at least two everyday examples, how a force can change an object's speed, direction, or shape.
✓
SHOULD  Describe pressure as force acting on a given area, and demonstrate with a simple test how changing the surface area changes the pressure.
✓
COULD  Compare contact and non-contact forces, and classify given real-life examples of each correctly.

INVESTIGATE FIRST  A drawing pin has a sharp tip and a wide flat head. Press the same pin into a soft eraser first with its head, then with its tip. Predict which way sinks in more easily, then inspect the two surfaces and note one reason for the difference.
I DO  Force is a push or pull. When a force acts on an area, pressure = force ÷ area. The pin's tip has a tiny area, so the same push creates much larger pressure and the pin sinks in. The wide head has a large area, so the pressure on your thumb is small and it does not hurt.
WE DO  Work through this example together. A box presses on the floor with a force of 60 N. Its base area is 0.3 m². Pressure = 60 ÷ 0.3 = 200 N/m². Now change the base area to 0.6 m² and calculate again. Explain in one line why the pressure changes even though the force is the same.
YOU DO  1. A book of weight 12 N rests on a cover of area 0.04 m². Calculate the pressure. 2. Give one everyday example where a small area is useful and one where a large area is useful. 3. Revise your prediction from the pin investigation using the pressure formula as evidence.

Higher Achievers task
A shop sign hangs from a single hook. Explain why a wider sign feels the same weight but presses on the wall with less pressure than a narrow sign, and suggest one design change to stop the hook pulling out of a soft wall.
Middle Achievers task
A box weighs 60 N and rests on a face with area 0.3 m². Calculate the pressure in N/m². Then explain why the same box presses harder on the floor when it stands on a smaller face.
Lower Achievers task
Pressure = force ÷ area. A book weighs 12 N and covers an area of 0.4 m². First write the numbers into the formula, then work out the pressure. Sentence starter: "The pressure is N/m² because the force is spread over m²."
Mini Plenary
Why does a sharp pin pierce a surface more easily than a blunt pin pushed with the same force?

deck.slideTitle: Real Life and Cross Curricular Connection
deck.body:
CONNECTION FOCUS  Real-Life Application — Force and Pressure in Everyday Tools
INVESTIGABLE QUESTION  Why does a sharp knife cut fruit more easily than a blunt one, even when you push with the same force?
PREDICT  On a scale of 1 to 5 (1 = not at all, 5 = very strongly), rate how much you think the area of contact affects the pressure produced by a force. Write your rating and one sentence explaining your reasoning.
INSPECT THE EVIDENCE  Look at these three everyday situations and record what you observe about the area of contact and the effect of the force.
A drawing pin has a sharp point at one end and a wide flat head at the other. When you push the pin, the point enters the wall easily but your thumb is not pierced by the flat head.
A school bag with wide shoulder straps feels more comfortable than one with thin straps, even when both bags carry the same books.
A snowshoe spreads a person's weight over a large area so they do not sink into soft snow, while a high-heeled shoe sinks into soft ground.
EXPLAIN THE PATTERN  Pressure = Force ÷ Area. When the same force acts on a smaller area, the pressure is greater. When it acts on a larger area, the pressure is smaller. Use this relationship to explain each observation above.
REVISE YOUR CLAIM  Return to your rating from the Predict step. Write your new rating and explain what evidence changed or supported your thinking.
Cross-Curricular Link — Mathematics: Calculate the pressure produced in each case. Use Pressure = Force ÷ Area and show your working with correct units (N/m² or Pa).
A force of 60 N acts on an area of 0.02 m² (sharp point of a drawing pin).
A force of 60 N acts on an area of 0.60 m² (flat head of the same pin).
Compare your two answers. Which area produces the greater pressure, and by how many times?

One Word Summary
OBJECTIVE  Capture the core idea of how force and pressure affect objects and everyday life in a single word, then justify your choice with evidence from today's lesson.
STEP 1  Think silently. Review the key ideas you explored: effects of force (change in speed, direction, shape), pressure as force spread over area, and applications such as sharp knives, wide snowshoes, and hydraulic brakes.
STEP 2  Write one word that best summarises the most important idea you learned about effects of force, pressure, and their applications. Write it large on your mini-whiteboard or in your notebook.
STEP 3  Write one sentence explaining why you chose that word. Use a specific example from today's lesson. For example: "Pressure — because a sharp knife has a small area so it exerts greater pressure and cuts easily."
STEP 4  Share your word and sentence with your partner. Listen to their word and sentence, then decide together which word best captures the lesson's big idea.
STEP 5  Be ready to share your word and sentence with the class when called.
